title: Subsystem Nesting Explorer
description: Open each of a car's four subsystems to see that every subsystem is a complete system in its own right.
creator: Systems Thinking in the Age of AI
author: Dan McCreary
subject: Systems Thinking in the Age of AI
Foundations of Systems Thinking

educational.learningObjective: Given a depicted car, the learner will differentiate the whole-car system from its nested subsystems and identify each subsystem's own inputs and outputs.
prerequisites: Knows the input / throughput / output vocabulary
Has seen at least one system boundary drawn
learningOutcomes: Differentiate a whole system from its nested subsystems
State the input, throughput and output of a given subsystem
Explain why one subsystem's output being another's input is what makes a system more than a pile of parts
educational.assessmentOpportunity: Ask each learner to pick any subsystem and write its input, throughput and output, then to name one other subsystem it depends on. The dependency is the part that shows real understanding.

pedagogical.interactionPattern: Click-to-expand progressive disclosure with animated transitions
pedagogical.instructionalStrategy: Structural analogy - the same three-part structure is shown at two levels of nesting
pedagogical.feedbackType: In-place expansion plus a definition panel on every click
misconceptionsAddressed: That a subsystem is somehow simpler or less complete than a system
That subsystems can be understood independently of each other
discussionQuestions: At what point does it stop being useful to keep decomposing a system into subsystems?
A dead battery stops a car with a perfectly good engine. What does that say about analyzing subsystems in isolation?
Is a department a subsystem of a company, or a system in its own right? Does the answer matter?
